title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 10: Addressing the ACID Problems of the Philippine Judiciary
keywords: Addressing the ACID Problems of the Philippine Judiciary
access to justice by the poor
Ang Bagong Bayani-OFW Labor Party v. Commission on Elections
primary_topics: Chapter 10 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- CJP's comprehensive progress report on the Action Program for Judicial Reform, organized around the four ACID problems he made the priority of his chief justiceship: limited access to justice by the poor, corruption, incompetence, and delay in the delivery of quality judgments.

His opening program restated: a judiciary of four Ins, impervious to the plague of 'ships,' a revitalized legal profession, and the DHL bargain with 26,000 judicial employees, all converging on the twin beacons of Liberty and Prosperity.

The justification of judicial reform as economic policy: stability and predictability in the dispensation of justice are a prerequisite for development, so speedy justice, democracy and the economy are intertwined in one tapestry of governance.

A catalogue of the concrete projects addressing each ACID letter -- pro-poor jurisprudence and Justice on Wheels; compensation reform and e-payment against corruption; bar, JBC, PhilJA and conduct-code reforms against incompetence; and the Zero Backlog committee and a wide computerization program against delay.
sub_topics: The December 21, 2005 vow: four Ins of independence, integrity, industry and intelligence, moral courage against influence, interference, indifference and insolence, and imperviousness to kinship, relationship, friendship and fellowship.
The pledge to continue and revitalize the APJR with focus on the four ACID problems, and the vision of a legal profession that is responsible, dependable and morally upright.
The internal bargain with 26,000 judicial employees: maximum lawful financial and fringe benefits in exchange for DHL -- dedication to duty, honesty in every way, and full loyalty.

The six-component APJR initiated in 2000 by his predecessor Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr., running from law-school curriculum and bar examinations through professional standards, nominations, continuing education, discipline, compensation and institutional development.

International and private support for the APJR: UNDP, the World Bank, ADB, the European Union, national aid agencies of Australia, Canada, Great Britain, Japan, the Netherlands and the United States, and grants from The Asia Foundation, the ABA-Asia Law Initiative, Role and the Judicial Institutes of Australia and Canada.

The pro-poor Constitution: free access to courts and legal assistance that 'shall not be denied to any person by reason of poverty,' Miranda rights, due process and counsel, and social justice high in the constitutional hierarchy, implemented by laws on detainees, women and children, housing, agriculture and labor.
The Court's own opening of the justice system to indigents: exemption from docket fees and transcripts, free counsel, required pro bono representation, and subsidy to the IBP Free Legal Aid program.

Pro-poor jurisprudence: Ang Bagong Bayani-OFW Labor Party v. Comelec reserving the party-list system for the marginalized, and the labor-law line running back to the 1940 seeds of Calalang v. Williams.

Human-rights enforcement: penalizing judges who failed to inform uneducated accused of the right to counsel, annulling judgments lacking a 'searching inquiry,' voiding judgments not conforming to constitutional form and substance, and extending the Universal Declaration's protection to aliens.

Diagnostic and participatory studies of the Department of Justice, penal institutions and jails, plus the IBP jail decongestion project with UNDP funding in Manila, Pasay, Quezon City and Pasig City jails.
The EU-assisted project strengthening courts for internally displaced persons, part of a program to rehabilitate at least 10,000 displaced families in Southern Philippines.
Justice on Wheels, launched December 21, 2004: large buses staffed by a judge, prosecutor and stenographer bringing courts to otherwise inaccessible places and helping decongest jails.

Combating corruption: strict entrance and promotion requirements, continuing ethical education, stricter discipline, and compensation reform under Republic Act 9227 doubling judicial pay by November 2006.

The compensation endgame: a requested lump-sum appropriation equal to a fixed percentage -- say two percent -- of the national budget, against a judiciary share now below one percent, plus exemption from the Salary Standardization Law.

Bar examination reforms adopted June 8, 2004: a tenured board of examiners, character and fitness investigation, multiple-choice questions alongside essays, scaling for test equity, and eventual computerization.
Mandatory Continuing Legal Education requiring training hours including legal ethics before license renewal.

The Judicial and Bar Council's three S tasks -- search, screen and select -- with the activist search added on his initiative, constant dialogues, the 29.49 percent end-2005 vacancy rate, and the website opened April 21, 2006.
Judicial education through PhilJA and the Japanese government's P300 million grant for the Tagaytay training center, handed over by Ambassador Ryuichiro Yamazaki on January 26, 2006.

Codes of conduct enforced: 463 lawyers sanctioned in six years under the Code of Professional Responsibility, the New Code of Judicial Conduct adopted June 1, 2004 after the Bangalore Principles, and 660 justices and judges penalized from 1999 to 2004.

Judicial Excellence Awards begun by the Foundation for Judicial Excellence in 1991, taken over by the Court in 2004 and handed in 2006 to the Society for Judicial Excellence he helped organize in 2005; plus new rules on electronic evidence, intellectual property, corporate rehabilitation, juveniles and violence against women.
'Justice-to-Justice' and 'Judge-to-Judge' Dialogues funded by USAID through the ABA-Asia Law Initiative.
Attacking delay: the Committee on Zero Backlog created on his assumption of office to monitor case flow and prioritize old cases.

Court technology: the USAID-supported Case Flow Management system pilot-tested in Pasay City, the CIDA-supported CAMIS turned over May 8, 2006, the Sandiganbayan's complete computerization launched March 14, 2006 covering 2,700 cases, and the e-library launched November 19, 2004 and extended to law schools on February 20, 2006.

Computer literacy for 28,000 judicial officials and employees, a personal computer in every courtroom, and an interest-free P1,000-per-month laptop installment program extended under his watch to rank-and-file employees.

The Benchbook for Trial Court Judges and the Manual of Judicial Writing; World Bank-assisted model electronic courts in Angeles, Lapulapu and Cagayan de Oro; and the Arroceros GSIS building to be converted into a modern hall of justice.

The pilot e-payment system inaugurated April 21, 2006 in Quezon City and Makati, remitting fees directly to Land Bank, funding the RA 9227 pay increase and freeing clerks of court from the temptations of holding cash.
The April 6, 2006 PLDT agreement to connect Metro Manila courts to the Internet by BizDSL, to be extended nationwide.

stances.claim: Judicial reform is economic policy: stability and predictability in the dispensation of justice are a prerequisite for economic development, so speedy justice, democracy and the economy are intertwined in one tapestry of governance.
stances.rhetorical_move: premise-of-the-program framing, offered as the proposition on which the entire APJR was crafted

stances.claim: The Philippine Constitution and Supreme Court are openly and unabashedly pro-poor, pro-labor and pro-human rights, nowhere more clearly than in labor law decisions.
stances.rhetorical_move: declaration backed by a long line of cases, with Ang Bagong Bayani quoted at length and Calalang v. Williams invoked as the root

stances.claim: Corruption is not only direct bribery; it hides behind Filipino cultural and family ties in the form of the plague of 'ships,' so the remedies must be structural -- strict entry and promotion standards, ethical education, discipline and adequate compensation.
stances.rhetorical_move: redefinition of the problem to justify a set of indirect, institutional remedies rather than prosecutions alone

stances.claim: The judiciary needs a lump-sum appropriation equal to a fixed percentage of the national budget -- say two percent, against a share now below one percent -- and exemption from the Salary Standardization Law, to settle judicial compensation permanently.
stances.rhetorical_move: gratitude-then-ask: he credits RA 9227 before pressing Congress for the structural fiscal remedy

stances.claim: Reducing the judicial vacancy rate through appointment of the best and brightest will solve not only the 'I' for incompetence but also the 'D' for delay, making recruitment the lever on two ACID problems at once.
stances.rhetorical_move: single-lever argument linking two of his four named problems to one reform

notable_anecdotes: Justice on Wheels, launched December 21, 2004: the first three mobile courts were large buses staffed by a judge, a prosecutor and a stenographer, designed to bring courts to places that would otherwise be inaccessible.

The Sandiganbayan computerization he inaugurated on March 14, 2006, after which any of the anti-graft court's 2,700 pending cases could be accessed electronically -- the step that would make the judiciary 'paperless.'
The interest-free P1,000-per-month installment program enabling justices and judges to own personal laptops, which under his watch was expanded to rank-and-file employees.
The clerks of court who had 'borrowed' from fee collections and were dismissed or heavily fined, cited as the reason the new e-payment system routes fees directly to Land Bank.
His helping organize the Society for Judicial Excellence in 2005, composed of all previous Judicial Excellence Awardees, to which the annual Search was turned over in 2006.
The P300 million check for the PhilJA Training Center in Tagaytay handed over by Japanese Ambassador Ryuichiro Yamazaki on January 26, 2006.
The disciplinary tally he reports without softening: 463 lawyers sanctioned in six years and 660 justices and judges penalized between 1999 and 2004.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' set out Chief Justice Panganiban's full programmatic report on the Action Program for Judicial Reform, arranged by the four ACID problems he had made his priority. He restated his December 21, 2005 vow of a judiciary marked by four Ins -- independence, integrity, industry and intelligence -- impervious to the plague of 'ships,' his vision of a revitalized legal profession, and the DHL bargain with 26,000 judicial employees, all converging on the twin beacons of Liberty and Prosperity. He described the six-component APJR his predecessor Chief Justice Davide had begun in 2000 and the international and private support behind it, resting the whole enterprise on the proposition that speedy justice, democracy and the economy are intertwined in one tapestry of governance. On access, he called the Constitution pro-poor, pro-labor and pro-human rights, catalogued the Court's exemptions and free counsel for indigents, quoted Ang Bagong Bayani-OFW Labor Party v. Comelec on the party-list system as a social justice vehicle, invoked the labor line from Calalang v. Williams, and reported jail studies, the IBP decongestion project, the EU project for internally displaced persons and the Justice on Wheels mobile courts. On corruption, he described it as hiding behind kinship and friendship and answered it with entry standards, ethical education, discipline and Republic Act 9227's doubling of judicial pay, while asking Congress for a lump-sum appropriation of about two percent of the national budget and exemption from the Salary Standardization Law. On incompetence, he reported the June 2004 bar reforms, the MCLE, the JBC's three S tasks and 29.49 percent vacancy rate, PhilJA and the P300 million Japanese grant, the New Code of Judicial Conduct patterned on the Bangalore Principles, and the sanctioning of 463 lawyers and 660 judges. On delay, he described the Committee on Zero Backlog and a broad computerization program, from case flow management and CAMIS to the Sandiganbayan's paperless docket, the e-library, model electronic courts, e-payment and broadband connectivity.
